glossary.short: A group of reps done in a row without resting.
glossary.long: A set is one round of an exercise. You do a number of reps, then you put the weight down and rest. Three sets of 10 reps means ten reps, rest, ten reps, rest, ten reps.

glossary.short: One full lift of the weight, up and back down.
glossary.long: A rep is one complete movement, for example lowering yourself in a push-up and pushing back up. You count reps to know how much work a set was.

glossary.short: How many more reps you could have done when you stopped.
glossary.long: If you stop a set and could have done 2 more clean reps, that set was 2 RIR. Most working sets should be 1 to 3 RIR: hard, but not to the point of failure.

glossary.short: The point where you cannot do another rep with good form.
glossary.long: Training to failure means you keep going until the next rep will not move. It is tiring and slows recovery, so use it rarely and mostly on safe exercises.

glossary.short: The heaviest weight you could lift for exactly one rep.
glossary.long: Most people never test it. The app can estimate it from a normal set, which is a safer way to compare strength over time.

glossary.short: The total amount of work: sets times reps, sometimes times weight.
glossary.long: More hard sets for a muscle each week usually means more growth, up to the point you can still recover. Three sets of 10 is 30 reps of volume.

glossary.short: The weight you lift.
glossary.long: Load is the number on the bar, plate stack or dumbbell. Raising load a little over time is how you keep getting stronger.

glossary.short: Doing slightly more over time so the body has a reason to adapt.
glossary.long: You can add a little weight, add a rep, or do the same weight with better control. Small steps every week or two beat big jumps.

glossary.short: Eating fewer calories than your body burns.
glossary.long: A deficit is the gap between what you eat and what you burn. Sustained over weeks, the body covers the gap with stored fat, so you lose weight.

glossary.short: Eating more calories than your body burns.
glossary.long: A surplus gives the body spare energy to build muscle and weight. A small one builds muscle with less fat gain than a big one.

glossary.short: The calories at which your weight stays the same.
glossary.long: Eat at maintenance and your weight holds. Eat below it to lose, above it to gain. It changes with weight, activity and age.

glossary.short: Total daily energy expenditure: all calories you burn in a day.
glossary.long: It adds up resting burn, digestion, walking, daily movement and exercise. It is the same idea as maintenance. The app estimates it from your body and refines it from your logs.

glossary.short: The calories your body burns at complete rest.
glossary.long: This is what you would burn lying in bed all day. It is the biggest part of what you burn, but not all of it.

glossary.short: The unit of food energy. Food labels say Calories or kcal, they are the same.
glossary.long: One kcal is a measure of energy. Everyone says calories in daily talk, and the app writes kcal.

glossary.short: One of the three big nutrients: protein, carbs and fat.
glossary.long: Every food is made of macros plus water and small things like vitamins. Protein and carbs give 4 kcal per gram, fat gives 9.

glossary.short: The nutrient that repairs and builds muscle.
glossary.long: Meat, fish, eggs, tofu and milk are good sources. Eating enough protein helps you keep muscle while losing fat.

glossary.short: The nutrient that is your body's easiest fuel.
glossary.long: Rice, bread, noodles, fruit and sugar are carbs. They fuel training and keep energy steady. They are not the enemy, they just need to fit your total.

glossary.short: The densest nutrient, 9 kcal per gram, needed for hormones and health.
glossary.long: Cooking oil, nuts, fatty meat and coconut milk carry fat. A little goes a long way in calories, so oil and sauces add up fast.

glossary.short: The part of plants you cannot digest, which keeps you full.
glossary.long: Vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains have fiber. It slows hunger and keeps digestion regular.

glossary.short: The band around a target that still counts as on target.
glossary.long: Hitting one exact number every day is not possible, so the app gives you a band. Inside it, you are In range and the day counts.

glossary.short: Your total for the day sits inside the target band.
glossary.long: The Food screen shows In range when your calories or a macro land inside the band. It means you are on target, not almost on target.

glossary.short: The share of your weight that is fat.
glossary.long: A body fat of 20 percent at 80 kg means about 16 kg of fat. Photos and the trend are used to estimate it.

glossary.short: Everything in your body that is not fat: muscle, bone, organs, water.
glossary.long: Lean mass is your weight minus fat mass. In a cut you want to keep it as high as possible.

glossary.short: The kilograms of fat your body carries.
glossary.long: Weight times body fat share. It is the number that should fall when a cut works.

glossary.short: Your weight with the daily ups and downs smoothed out.
glossary.long: Water, salt and food in your gut move the scale 1 to 2 kg a day. The trend looks at several weeks and shows the real direction.

glossary.short: Your best ever on an exercise.
glossary.long: A PR can be more weight, more reps or a better version of the same lift. It is a sign you are progressing.

glossary.short: Two exercises done back to back with no rest between them.
glossary.long: You do one set of the first exercise, go straight into the second, then rest. It saves time in a busy gym.

glossary.short: Lowering the weight right after a hard set and continuing.
glossary.long: You reach near failure, drop the weight by about 20 percent and keep going for more reps. It is tiring, so use it at the end of a session.

glossary.short: How fast you lift and lower the weight.
glossary.long: A slow, controlled lowering of 2 to 3 seconds makes the same weight harder and teaches control. Do not bounce the weight.

glossary.short: Easy movement and light sets that prepare you to lift heavy.
glossary.long: A few minutes of light cardio plus 1 or 2 light sets of the first exercise raise your body temperature and practise the movement.

glossary.short: A planned easy week to let your body recover.
glossary.long: You cut the weight or the sets by about half for a week. Many people feel stronger after it.

glossary.short: A lift that uses several joints and muscles at once.
glossary.long: Squat, bench press, row and deadlift are compound. They give the most strength for the time spent.

glossary.short: A lift that works mainly one muscle and one joint.
glossary.long: A biceps curl or leg extension are isolation. They finish off a muscle after the big lifts.

glossary.short: Muscle growth.
glossary.long: It is the word for making muscles bigger. It happens when you train a muscle hard enough, eat enough protein and recover.

glossary.short: How much force you can produce, usually the heaviest weight you can lift.
glossary.long: Strength mostly improves with heavier weights and lower reps. It also helps growth, as stronger muscles can be trained with more load.

glossary.short: Exercise that raises your heart rate for a while, like walking, running or cycling.
glossary.long: Cardio is good for the heart and burns calories. Walking counts, and it is easy to recover from.

glossary.short: The count of steps your phone or watch records during the day.
glossary.long: It is a simple way to measure daily movement. More steps means more calories burned outside the gym.

glossary.short: Calories burned by everyday movement that is not exercise.
glossary.long: Walking to the jeepney, cooking, cleaning and standing all count. For many people it is a bigger lever than the gym.

glossary.short: The pause between sets.
glossary.long: Rest 1 to 3 minutes for most lifts, longer for heavy ones. The app has a rest timer to track it.

glossary.short: Replacing an exercise with a similar one.
glossary.long: Swap when a machine is busy or something hurts. Pick one that trains the same muscle.

glossary.short: The time your body uses to repair after training.
glossary.long: Muscles grow while you rest, not while you lift. Sleep, food and days off are the recovery.

glossary.short: The way you do the movement.
glossary.long: Good form means controlled movement through the full range with a steady back. It protects joints and works the right muscle.

glossary.short: How far a joint moves in an exercise.
glossary.long: A full range, like a deep squat you can control, usually builds more than short half reps.

glossary.short: A stretch where progress stalls.
glossary.long: Weight or strength stops moving for a few weeks. Check sleep, food and whether you are adding load, before changing everything.

glossary.short: Losing fat and building muscle at the same time.
glossary.long: Possible for beginners and people returning to training. It works best with high protein, lifting and a small deficit.

glossary.short: How consistently you follow the plan.
glossary.long: The best plan is the one you keep doing. A decent plan done for a year beats a perfect plan done for two weeks.

lessons.title: What sets and reps are
lessons.summary: The two words behind every workout, in plain language.

cards.p: One rep is one full movement: lowering the weight and lifting it back. Lower yourself in a push-up, push back up, and that is one rep.
cards.example: Think of scooping rice from the pot: one full scoop is one rep.

cards.h: A set is a group of reps
cards.p: A set is a bunch of reps in a row. When you stop and rest, the set is over. 10 reps in a row is one set of 10.
cards.example: Ten push-ups, then you catch your breath. That was one set.

cards.p: The program says 3 x 10. That means 3 sets of 10 reps: do 10, rest, do 10, rest, do 10. That is 30 reps in total.
cards.example: Like three trips carrying 10 bottles of water each from the tindahan.

cards.p: Rest 1 to 3 minutes between sets so the next set is also good. The app has a rest timer that counts it for you.
cards.example: Rest about as long as it takes to drink water and check your phone, not to scroll for ten minutes.

lessons.title: Reps in reserve and how hard to push
lessons.summary: How to tell if a set was hard enough, and why you should not go to failure every time.

cards.p: RIR is how many more good reps you could still do when you stop. If you stop and could do 2 more, that set was 2 RIR.
cards.example: You carry groceries up the stairs and feel you could still do two more steps with good posture. That is 2 RIR.

cards.p: Most sets should end at 1 to 3 RIR. That is hard enough to grow, with enough left to stay safe and recover.
cards.example: If the last rep felt like a struggle but you stayed in control, you hit it.

cards.p: Failure is when you cannot do another rep. It is 0 RIR. Use it rarely, only on safe exercises, because it is very tiring.
cards.example: It is like sprinting for the last jeepney with nothing left. Great once in a while, not every day.

cards.p: After each set you can tell the app how many you had left. Several sets at 3 or more mean the weight is too light, so add some next time.
cards.example: If every set of bench felt easy this week, go up 2.5 kg next week.

check.q: You finish a set and could have done 2 more reps. What is the RIR?

lessons.title: Reading the workout screen
lessons.summary: Previous, rest timer, swap and add, what each button does.

cards.p: Each row is one set. You type the weight and the reps, then tick it. When you tick, the rest timer starts.
cards.example: Row 1 says 40 kg x 10. You did it, so you tick it.

cards.p: The column called Previous shows what you did last time on this set. It is your target to match or beat.
cards.example: Last time you did 40 kg x 8. Today try 40 kg x 9 or 10.

cards.p: After a tick, the timer counts your rest and beeps when it is over. You can skip it if you feel ready.
cards.example: Start the timer, drink water, wipe the machine, and by then it is over.

cards.p: Swap replaces an exercise with a similar one if the machine is busy or something hurts. Add lets you put in an extra exercise or set.
cards.example: The lat pulldown is taken, so swap it for another back exercise.

check.q: What does the Previous column show?
options: What you did last time on this set
What the app thinks you should lift
The weight on the empty bar

lessons.title: Calories and the deficit
lessons.summary: Why calories decide weight, and what a deficit is.

cards.p: A calorie, or kcal, is a unit of energy in food. Your body burns calories all day, even at rest.
cards.example: A cup of cooked rice is about 200 kcal.

cards.p: Maintenance is how many calories you burn in a day. Eat that and your weight stays the same.
cards.example: If you burn 2,200 and eat 2,200, the scale does not move.

cards.p: Eat less than maintenance and you are in a deficit, so the body uses stored fat. Eat more and you are in a surplus, so you gain.
cards.example: Burn 2,200, eat 1,700: a 500 kcal deficit, about half a kilo of fat lost every 2 weeks, roughly.

cards.p: A moderate deficit keeps your energy and muscle. Crash diets lose muscle and are hard to keep. The app sets a pace for you.
cards.example: Skipping rice for one week is not a plan. Eating a bit less rice every day for months is.

check.q: You eat fewer calories than you burn. What is that called?

lessons.title: Protein
lessons.summary: The nutrient that protects and builds muscle.

cards.p: Protein repairs muscle after training. In a deficit, enough protein helps you lose fat and keep muscle.
cards.example: Chicken breast, eggs, tuna and tofu are all protein.

cards.p: A common aim is about 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg of body weight a day. The app sets your target and a range that goes above it. More is fine.
cards.example: At 80 kg that is roughly 130 to 175 g.

cards.p: Spread protein across your meals, about 25 to 40 g each. It is easier than eating it all at dinner.
cards.example: Itlog at breakfast, adobo at lunch, grilled fish at dinner.

cards.p: Pick lean and cheap ones: eggs, chicken, tuna, tofu, milk, whey. Check the label for grams of protein, not just the front claim.
cards.example: A can of tuna is about 25 g of protein for a few pesos.

check.q: Why do you eat protein when cutting?

lessons.title: Reading the Food screen
lessons.summary: Ranges, In range, and what is left for the day.

cards.p: The top shows what you have eaten and what is left of your daily calories, plus protein, carbs and fat.
cards.example: After breakfast it says 1,300 kcal left.

cards.p: You do not need an exact number. Each target has a band around it, and a day inside the band counts as on target.
cards.example: If your target is 1,750 and you eat 1,820, you are still in range.

cards.p: When a number sits inside its band, the app shows In range. Outside, it shows how far you are over or under.
cards.example: Protein 160 g with a 165 g target is under. 170 g is in range.

cards.p: Use the command bar to type or say what you ate, or add a photo. Check the numbers, because estimates can be off.
cards.example: Type '2 cups rice, adobo 150g' and the app fills it in.

check.q: Your target is 1,750 kcal and you ate 1,800. What does the app show?

lessons.title: Steps and walking
lessons.summary: Daily steps are the easiest way to burn more.

cards.p: Walking burns calories without tiring you for the next workout. It adds up over a whole day.
cards.example: Walking to the jeepney stop and back can be 2,000 steps.

cards.p: The app has a daily step goal, often 8,000 to 10,000. It is a target, not a test. Any increase helps.
cards.example: If you do 5,000 now, aim for 6,500 first.

cards.p: Take stairs, get off one stop early, walk after meals, take a call on your feet.
cards.example: A 10-minute walk after lunch is about 1,000 steps.

cards.p: Your phone counts them. You can type them in or send a screenshot, and the Android helper app can sync them each hour.
cards.example: Open your health app, copy the number, enter it before bed.

check.q: Which is the simplest way to raise your daily burn?

lessons.title: Progressive overload
lessons.summary: The one idea that makes you keep improving.

cards.p: Your body only grows or gets stronger if it has a reason to. Doing a little more than before gives it that reason. This is progressive overload.
cards.example: Carrying one gallon of water is easy. Carrying two every day for a month makes the first one feel light.

cards.p: Add a little weight, add a rep, or do the same thing with better control. Any of them counts.
cards.example: Last week 10 reps at 40 kg. This week 11 reps, or 10 reps at 42.5 kg.

cards.p: Go up in small steps. About 2.5 kg for big lifts, 1 to 2 kg for small ones, or one extra rep. Do it when all your sets feel easy.
cards.example: If you hit all your reps with 3 RIR, go up a little next time.

cards.p: If you cannot add anything for two or three weeks, check sleep, food and stress. Do not just add more exercises.
cards.example: You slept 5 hours all week on a night shift. That is why the bar did not move.

check.q: All your sets felt easy with 3 reps in reserve. What now?
options: Add a little weight or a rep next time

lessons.title: Carbs and fat
lessons.summary: The other two macros and why neither is bad.

cards.p: Carbs give quick energy for training and daily life. Rice, bread, fruit and noodles are carbs.
cards.example: 1 cup of cooked rice is about 45 g of carbs.

cards.p: Fat gives 9 kcal per gram, more than double protein or carbs. A little is needed for health, but it adds up fast.
cards.example: One tablespoon of cooking oil is about 120 kcal. Fried foods hide a lot of it.

cards.p: After protein, your carbs and fat share the remaining calories. Some people feel better with more carbs, some with more fat.
cards.example: Adobo with a cup of rice is a good balance of protein, carbs and fat.

cards.p: Cutting all carbs or all fat is not needed. Stay inside the range for each and your results will come.
cards.example: You can keep rice. Just measure it.

check.q: How many kcal does 1 gram of fat have?

lessons.title: Rest, sleep and recovery
lessons.summary: Muscle grows when you rest, not when you lift.

cards.p: The workout tells the body to grow. The growing itself happens afterward, while you rest and eat.
cards.example: You paint a wall in the day. The paint dries overnight.

cards.p: Aim for 7 to 9 hours. Poor sleep means more hunger, less strength and worse mood.
cards.example: Two nights of 4 hours and you crave sweets all day. That is normal.

cards.p: Take at least 1 or 2 days a week off from lifting. Easy walking is fine. Sore is normal, sharp pain is not.
cards.example: Sunday with the family is a good rest day.

cards.p: Every 6 to 10 weeks, if you feel run down, do a lighter week. Use half the weight or half the sets.
cards.example: After a busy month at work, a lighter week can bring your strength back.

check.q: When do your muscles actually grow?

lessons.title: Warm-up and form basics
lessons.summary: How to start a session and keep lifts safe.

cards.p: Spend 5 minutes on light cardio, then do 1 or 2 light sets of your first exercise. It lets joints move freely.
cards.example: Walk briskly for 5 minutes, then do an empty-bar bench press.

cards.p: Lift with control, lower slowly, do not bounce. If you have to swing, the weight is too heavy.
cards.example: Count 'one, two' on the way down.

cards.p: Move through a full range you can control. Short half reps give you less.
cards.example: Squat as deep as you can without your back rounding.

cards.p: Muscle burn is fine. Sharp or joint pain is a stop sign. Swap the exercise or lower the weight and ask a coach.
cards.example: A sharp pinch in your shoulder means stop and pick a different press.

check.q: What should you do on sharp joint pain?
options: Stop and swap or lower the weight

lessons.title: Weight trend and progress photos
lessons.summary: Why one weigh-in lies, and how to see real change.

cards.p: Water, salt and food in your gut can move the scale 1 to 2 kg in a day. One weigh-in tells you very little.
cards.example: After salty food and a late dinner, you are heavier by morning. Fat did not grow overnight.

cards.p: Weigh in the same way, ideally each morning. The app draws a trend line through several weeks. That line is the real direction.
cards.example: The dots jump around, the line goes down slowly. Trust the line.

cards.p: Take photos once a week, same light, same pose, same time. They show change that the scale hides, especially when you lose fat and build muscle together.
cards.example: Front, side and back, every Sunday morning before breakfast.

cards.p: Real change shows over 3 to 4 weeks. If the trend is flat for 3 to 4 weeks, adjust food a little. Do not change on day three.
cards.example: Give the plan a month before you judge it.

check.q: Which is the best way to read your weight?
